The detected absorption line has an energy of \(3.9 \times 10^{-6}\) eV. Converting this to frequency using \(E = h\nu\) (with \(h \approx 4.136 \times 10^{-15}\) eV·s) gives \(\nu \approx 9.43 \times 10^8\) Hz (943 MHz), corresponding to a wavelength of about 32 cm. This is very close to the redshifted 21 cm line of neutral atomic hydrogen (HI), which has a rest frequency of 1420 MHz (\(5.9 \times 10^{-6}\) eV). A source at 2.1 Gpc has a cosmological redshift \(z \approx 0.5\), which shifts the 21 cm line to \(1420 / (1+0.5) \approx 947\) MHz, matching the observed energy.

The 21 cm line traces neutral atomic hydrogen, not molecular gas (eliminating options B and D). While warm atomic medium emits broadly, strong, narrow 21 cm absorption features are predominantly associated with cold atomic clouds (the Cold Neutral Medium, CNM) in the Milky Way. Therefore, this absorption line is most likely probing the cold atomic interstellar medium.

Answer: C
